subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Inflammatory bowel disease: Crohn vs ulcerative colitis
vignette: A 27-year-old woman has had 8 months of intermittent diarrhea, weight loss, and perianal pain. Colonoscopy shows discrete ulcerated segments separated by normal mucosa, with rectal sparing. Small bowel imaging shows thickened bowel wall and a narrowed segment.
question: Which pattern of disease best fits these findings?

options.text: Ulcerative colitis with continuous rectal involvement and loss of haustra
Microscopic colitis with normal-appearing mucosa on endoscopy
Irritable bowel syndrome with no structural abnormality
Crohn disease with skip lesions, transmural inflammation, and rectal sparing
Colonic ischemia at the splenic flexure watershed area

explanation_correct: Crohn disease can affect any portion of the GI tract, most often the terminal ileum and colon. It produces skip lesions with rectal sparing, transmural inflammation, cobblestone mucosa, creeping fat, bowel wall thickening with a string sign, linear ulcers, and fissures. Perianal disease is a common complication.

explanation_incorrect.A: Ulcerative colitis is continuous and always involves the rectum; it lacks skip lesions and transmural inflammation.
explanation_incorrect.B: Microscopic colitis causes chronic watery diarrhea but the colonic mucosa appears normal on endoscopy, without ulcers or wall thickening.
explanation_incorrect.C: Irritable bowel syndrome has no structural or inflammatory abnormalities and would not produce ulcers, weight loss, or perianal disease.
explanation_incorrect.E: Colonic ischemia occurs at watershed areas in older adults with crampy pain followed by hematochezia and a thumbprint sign, not chronic skip lesions.

educationalObjective: Crohn disease features skip lesions, transmural inflammation, and rectal sparing, unlike continuous ulcerative colitis.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Inflammatory bowel disease: Crohn vs ulcerative colitis
vignette: A 35-year-old man with long-standing Crohn disease develops recurrent urinary tract infections and passes air in the urine. Imaging shows a communication between the terminal ileum and the bladder.
question: Which underlying pathologic feature of Crohn disease most directly explains this complication?

options.text: Mucosal and submucosal inflammation confined to the colon
Crypt abscesses with surface ulceration and loss of haustra
Villous atrophy with intraepithelial lymphocytosis in the small bowel
PAS-positive macrophages infiltrating the intestinal lamina propria
Transmural inflammation with fistula formation

explanation_correct: Crohn disease is characterized by transmural inflammation, which predisposes to fistula formation. An enterovesical fistula allows intestinal gas and bacteria to enter the urinary tract, causing recurrent UTIs and pneumaturia. Other complications include phlegmon or abscess, strictures with obstruction, and perianal disease.

explanation_incorrect.A: Inflammation limited to mucosa and submucosa is characteristic of ulcerative colitis, which does not form transmural fistulas.
explanation_incorrect.B: Crypt abscesses and loss of haustra are features of ulcerative colitis, not the transmural process that produces an enterovesical fistula.
explanation_incorrect.C: Villous atrophy with intraepithelial lymphocytes is celiac disease and does not produce fistulas.
explanation_incorrect.D: PAS-positive foamy macrophages are the hallmark of Whipple disease, not Crohn disease.

educationalObjective: Transmural inflammation in Crohn disease causes fistulas, including enterovesical fistulas with pneumaturia.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Inflammatory bowel disease: Crohn vs ulcerative colitis
vignette: A 41-year-old woman presents with 3 months of bloody, painful diarrhea and urgency. Colonoscopy shows continuous inflammation beginning at the rectum and extending proximally, with friable mucosa and shallow ulcerations. Barium imaging shows loss of haustra with a lead-pipe appearance.
question: Which histologic finding would most likely be seen on biopsy?

options.text: Noncaseating granulomas with lymphoid aggregates
Crypt abscesses without granulomas
PAS-positive foamy macrophages in the lamina propria
Transmural inflammation with creeping fat
Thickened subepithelial collagen band

explanation_correct: Ulcerative colitis is a continuous colonic inflammation that always involves the rectum, producing friable mucosa, superficial and deep ulcerations, crypt abscesses, bleeding, and loss of haustra with a lead-pipe appearance. Granulomas are absent, which helps distinguish it from Crohn disease.

explanation_incorrect.A: Noncaseating granulomas are the histologic hallmark of Crohn disease, which has skip lesions rather than continuous rectal disease.
explanation_incorrect.C: PAS-positive foamy macrophages characterize Whipple disease, not ulcerative colitis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Transmural inflammation and creeping fat are features of Crohn disease; ulcerative colitis involves only mucosa and submucosa.
explanation_incorrect.E: A thickened subepithelial collagen band is seen in collagenous colitis, a form of microscopic colitis with normal endoscopy.

educationalObjective: Ulcerative colitis shows continuous rectal inflammation with crypt abscesses and no granulomas.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Inflammatory bowel disease: Crohn vs ulcerative colitis
vignette: A 24-year-old man undergoes biopsy of a strictured terminal ileum. Microscopy shows aggregates of epithelioid histiocytes without central necrosis, surrounded by lymphocytes. The surrounding mucosa shows transmural inflammation.
question: Which serologic marker is most strongly associated with this form of inflammatory bowel disease?

options.text: Antimitochondrial antibody
Anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA antibody
p-ANCA (MPO-ANCA)
Anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibody (ASCA)
Anti-smooth muscle antibody

explanation_correct: Noncaseating granulomas with transmural inflammation in the terminal ileum indicate Crohn disease. ASCA (anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibodies) may be positive in Crohn disease, whereas p-ANCA/MPO-ANCA is associated with ulcerative colitis. Neither is fully sensitive or specific enough for screening.

explanation_incorrect.A: Antimitochondrial antibody is associated with primary biliary cholangitis, not inflammatory bowel disease.
explanation_incorrect.B: Anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA antibody is the serologic hallmark of celiac disease.
explanation_incorrect.C: p-ANCA/MPO-ANCA is associated with ulcerative colitis and primary sclerosing cholangitis, not Crohn disease.
explanation_incorrect.E: Anti-smooth muscle antibody is associated with autoimmune hepatitis, not Crohn disease.

educationalObjective: Crohn disease may be ASCA-positive; p-ANCA is associated with ulcerative colitis.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Inflammatory bowel disease: Crohn vs ulcerative colitis
vignette: A 38-year-old woman with extensive ulcerative colitis presents with 5 days of bloody diarrhea, severe abdominal pain, and abdominal distention. A abdominal radiograph shows marked colonic dilation. She is at risk of colonic perforation.
question: Which complication is most characteristic of this presentation?

options.text: Enterovesical fistula with pneumaturia
Perianal disease with skin tags and fistula-in-ano
Calcium oxalate kidney stones from fat malabsorption
Small bowel stricture causing intermittent obstruction
Toxic megacolon

explanation_correct: Fulminant ulcerative colitis can lead to toxic megacolon, a life-threatening complication in which severe inflammation and edema cause massive colonic dilation with risk of perforation. Other complications of ulcerative colitis include perforation and an increased risk of colorectal cancer with pancolitis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Enterovesical fistula results from transmural Crohn disease, not ulcerative colitis, which is limited to mucosa and submucosa.
explanation_incorrect.B: Perianal disease is characteristic of Crohn disease; ulcerative colitis spares the perianal region.
explanation_incorrect.C: Calcium oxalate stones can complicate Crohn disease with ileal fat malabsorption; they are not a feature of acute severe colitic illness.
explanation_incorrect.D: Small bowel strictures are a complication of transmural Crohn disease; ulcerative colitis is confined to the colon.

educationalObjective: Toxic megacolon is a severe complication of ulcerative colitis with colonic dilation and perforation risk.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Inflammatory bowel disease: Crohn vs ulcerative colitis
vignette: Two patients with inflammatory bowel disease are being evaluated: one has chronic bloody diarrhea with continuous colonic involvement and p-ANCA positivity; the other has noncaseating granulomas and ASCA positivity. Both report eye inflammation and painful skin nodules.
question: Which extra-intestinal manifestations can occur in BOTH forms of inflammatory bowel disease?

options.text: Pyoderma gangrenosum, erythema nodosum, episcleritis or uveitis, aphthous stomatitis, and arthritis
Toxic megacolon and continuous rectal involvement only
Primary sclerosing cholangitis and p-ANCA positivity only
Noncaseating granulomas and skip lesions only
Enterovesical fistula and perianal disease only

explanation_correct: Both Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis share extra-intestinal manifestations: pyoderma gangrenosum, erythema nodosum, eye inflammation (episcleritis, uveitis), aphthous stomatitis, and arthritis (peripheral or spondylitis). Primary sclerosing cholangitis is more strongly associated with ulcerative colitis; calcium oxalate stones are more typical of Crohn disease.

explanation_incorrect.B: Toxic megacolon and continuous rectal involvement are features of ulcerative colitis, not shared manifestations, and toxic megacolon is an intestinal complication.
explanation_incorrect.C: Primary sclerosing cholangitis and p-ANCA are associated especially with ulcerative colitis, not both forms equally.
explanation_incorrect.D: Noncaseating granulomas and skip lesions define Crohn disease rather than being shared extra-intestinal features.
explanation_incorrect.E: Enterovesical fistula and perianal disease are transmural complications of Crohn disease, not ulcerative colitis.

educationalObjective: Pyoderma gangrenosum, erythema nodosum, uveitis, aphthous ulcers, and arthritis occur in both Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Inflammatory bowel disease: Crohn vs ulcerative colitis
vignette: A 30-year-old woman with known ulcerative colitis reports increased stool frequency and bleeding. Her physician wants an objective measure of intestinal inflammation to distinguish active IBD from irritable bowel syndrome and to monitor treatment response.
question: Which stool marker is most appropriate?

options.text: Stool occult blood alone, because it is specific for inflammatory colitis
Fecal fat (Sudan stain), because steatorrhea reflects colonic inflammation
Fecal calprotectin, because it reflects intestinal inflammation and distinguishes IBD from noninflammatory disease
Stool pH, because colonic fermentation predicts disease activity
Hydrogen breath test, because it detects bacterial overgrowth in IBD

explanation_correct: Fecal calprotectin is used to monitor IBD disease activity and to distinguish inflammatory disease such as IBD from noninflammatory conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome. Treatment of IBD includes glucocorticoids, azathioprine, biologics such as infliximab or adalimumab, and 5-aminosalicylic acid preparations for ulcerative colitis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Occult blood is not specific for inflammation and cannot reliably distinguish active IBD from other causes or from noninflammatory disease.
explanation_incorrect.B: Fecal fat testing evaluates malabsorption, not colonic inflammation, and is not used to monitor IBD activity.
explanation_incorrect.D: Stool pH reflects carbohydrate fermentation and is used in lactose intolerance, not IBD monitoring.
explanation_incorrect.E: Hydrogen breath testing evaluates lactose malabsorption or bacterial overgrowth, not intestinal inflammation.

educationalObjective: Fecal calprotectin monitors IBD activity and helps distinguish inflammatory bowel disease from irritable bowel syndrome.
